We discuss how mandatory licensing may provide a setting that aligns the dynamic incentives of rightsholders and AI developers.

title: The Self-Financing State: An Institutional Analysis of Government Expenditure, Revenue Collection and Debt Issuance Operations in the United Kingdom
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University College London - Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose and The Gower Initiative for Modern Money Studies

detail.title: The Self-Financing State: An Institutional Analysis of Government Expenditure, Revenue Collection and Debt Issuance Operations in the United Kingdom
detail.abstract: This article provides the first detailed institutional analysis of the UK government's expenditure, revenue collection, and debt issuance processes. We show that public expenditure is always financed through money creation rather than taxation or debt issuance. Spending involves the government drawing on a sovereign line of credit from a core legal and accounting structure known as the Consolidated Fund (CF). The Bank of England then debits the CF's account at the Bank and credits other government accounts held at the Bank. This creates new public deposits, which are used to settle spending by government departments via the commercial banking sector. Only the UK parliament can mandate expenditures from the CF. Revenue collection, including taxation, involves the reverse process, crediting the CF's account at the Bank, offsetting past injections. Similarly, gilts have been issued to temporarily withdraw money to assist monetary policy objectives. Under the current conditions of excess reserve liquidity, however, debt issuance is best understood as a way of providing safe assets and secure collateral to the non-bank private sector. The findings support neo-Chartalist accounts of the workings of sovereign currency-issuing nations and provide additional institutional detail regarding the apex of the monetary hierarchy in the UK.

title: A Corrected Measure of Orthogonalized Monetary Policy Surprises
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD)

detail.title: A Corrected Measure of Orthogonalized Monetary Policy Surprises
detail.abstract: This note reassesses the orthogonalized monetary policy surprises series proposed by Bauer and Swanson (2023a). Their approach aggregates daily FOMC surprises to the monthly level and only afterwards orthogonalizes them with respect to a subset of contemporaneous news variables. Instead, I purge each FOMC-day surprise from all available news releases before aggregation. The fully orthogonalized series loses instrumental strength and yields no significant responses in any of the macroeconomic variables under analysis, casting doubt either on the usefulness of the measure or, if taken seriously, on monetary non-neutrality. A simple model featuring explicit timing of the orthogonalization rationalizes the stark empirical differences.

title: Multidimensional Assessment of Sustainability: Harmony vs. the Turning Point
affiliations: Environment Europe Foundation

detail.title: Multidimensional Assessment of Sustainability: Harmony vs. the Turning Point
detail.abstract: Multidimensional assessment of sustainability is a way to reconcile the need for simultaneous consideration of various indicators of progress beyond GDP growth with a policy focused visualization of multi-dimensional trends in a clear and transparent manner. The various composite measures used for sustainability assessment often hide the trade-offs between economic, social and environmental dimensions of sustainability. This chapter discusses indicators used for sustainability analysis at the macro scale and offers a multi-criteria sustainability assessment framework. It discusses results that were obtained in sustainability assessments for the USA, Brazil, China, France, Germany, Britain and Russia. The Multicriteria Decision Aid tool, Aggregated Preference Index System (APIS) is used for the assessment with the following three headline indicators: GDP per capita; CO 2 emissions and Life Expectancy at birth. The indicators represent economic, environmental and social dimensions respectively. The multidimensional assessment is designed with two different policy priorities: priority of economic over environmental and social dimension versus priority of environmental and social dimensions over economic. Results help to identify countries, where economic development happened at the expense of environmental and social dimension and lead to policy conclusions.

title: All the Different faces of The Palestinian Right of Return
affiliations: University of Kent

detail.title: All the Different faces of The Palestinian Right of Return
detail.abstract: This Legal Analysis provides an overview of the Palestinian right of return in international law

title: Should We Use Central Bank Asset Purchase Announcements and Sign Restrictions to Quantify Quantitative Easing?
affiliations: University of the German Federal Armed Forces - Helmut Schmidt Universität

detail.title: Should We Use Central Bank Asset Purchase Announcements and Sign Restrictions to Quantify Quantitative Easing?
detail.abstract: The empirical literature lacks a consensus on how to model quantitative easing (QE) within the structural vector autoregression (SVAR) framework. As agents may anticipate central-bank balance sheet variables, the use of asset purchase announcements has become a common practice. I show that results derived from such SVAR models, identified with sign restrictions, should be cautiously interpreted. Structural shocks deemed to identify QE rather recover a different mechanism possibly related to monetary policy.

title: Information Technology, the State and the Voter in the Kenyan Election of2013
affiliations: University of New Mexico School of Law and Independent

detail.title: Information Technology, the State and the Voter in the Kenyan Election of2013
detail.abstract:
The importance of information and communication technologies in Kenya reached new heights during the March 2013 elections. Information and communication technologies (ICTs) were used in the general elections to encourage voting, provide information about candidates, promote "peace speech," and, on the negative side, intimidate voters, such as instructing them not to vote. In addition, new ICTs were introduced by the Government of Kenya (GoK) to improve

the accuracy of the election, as well as to control how people communicated about the election.

title: Circular Supply Chain Practices in Kochi: A Sustainable Transformation of the E-Commerce Logistics Sector
affiliations: Jain Deemed to be University and Christ University

detail.title: Circular Supply Chain Practices in Kochi: A Sustainable Transformation of the E-Commerce Logistics Sector
detail.abstract: E-commerce Industry has the strongest contributors to India's Economy, giving the strong support to the retail supply chain through fast logistics, warehouses automation, and technology focused last-mile delivery. Now this transformation is more visible in Kochi, Kerala's commercial capital, where rising incomes, deep digital focused setup, and the rapid growth of tech professionals into tech hubs like Infopark and Smart City have fuelled online retail growth. However, this massive expansion comes at an environmental cost. Now Kochi is facing an unprecedented surge in waste corrugated boxes, single-use plastic packaging, bubble wraps, multi-layer films, and non-recyclable laminates from huge deliveries. In the era of "take-make-dispose" linear model, these packing materials majorly end up in landfills, illegal dumps, or unsafe land reclamation sites, releasing toxins for decades. Due to Kochi's limited land availability, ecologically sensitive backwaters, and increased population create this challenge more acute. Circular Supply Chain (CSC) models focused on reuse, repair, refurbishment, and recycling-offer a way to play win-win situation both economic growth and environmental responsibility. Global players like Amazon, UPS and Geodis have successfully adopted CSC strategies such as closed-loop logistics and reusable packaging. In India, Flipkart's reverse logistics shows how circular supply chain can recover materials, cut waste, and create green jobs. Flipkart's Kochi Reverse Logistics Centre has started operational feasibility: barcode/QR code tracking for recovered goods, automated refurbishment triage, partnerships with certified recyclers, reduced transport emissions, and recovered packaging reuse. Emerging opportunities like climate-specific biodegradable packaging, AI waste sorting, blockchain product tracking, and neighbourhood take-back networks can position Kochi as a model circular city. The way forward lies in strong policy support, local innovation, and consumer participation.

title: Policy Frameworks for Sustainable Public Procurement: Global Trends and Local Adaptations
affiliations: University of Abuja, Abuja Nigeria, University of Abuja, Abuja Nigeria and University of Abuja

detail.title: Policy Frameworks for Sustainable Public Procurement: Global Trends and Local Adaptations
detail.abstract: Public procurement represents a significant portion of public expenditure worldwide, accounting for approximately 15-20 percent of total global GDP. This article will examine the evolving policy frameworks of sustainable public procurement (SPP) practices and the localisation of global trends across diverse jurisdictions. This research study used a qualitative methodology to assess the efficacy of current SPP frameworks, the problems associated with their implementation, and their potential to enhance the sustainability of procurement processes. The research indicates that while international norms are essential, tailored techniques must be established prior to successful implementation, contingent upon local economic, social, and environmental factors. Critical observations indicate that the adoption of SPP is prevalent in nations that have established comprehensive legal frameworks supported by efficient implementation guidelines and capacity building initiatives. However, challenges persist in the domain, including economic considerations, supplier competencies, and the assessment of sustainability outcomes. The study elucidates the methods by which policy frameworks can be developed to promote sustainable procurement practices that address local desires and constraints. Proposed recommendations include developing integrated policy solutions, augmenting institutional capacity, and creating conducive circumstances for the success of sustainable suppliers. This study provides valuable insights for policymakers, procurement professionals, and researchers to facilitate a more sustainable approach to government purchasing globally.

reference: Journal of Sport Management, volume 39, issue 5, 2025[10.1123/jsm.2024-0371]
title: Economic Impact, Fiscal Loss, and Redistribution of Wealth in Sport Events
affiliations: and University of Windsor

detail.title: Economic Impact, Fiscal Loss, and Redistribution of Wealth in Sport Events

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Sport Management, volume 39, issue 5, 2025[10.1123/jsm.2024-0371]

detail.abstract: This conceptual paper identifies erroneous economic impact reports as the first link in a chain reaction that can lead local governments to provide public subsidies to sport events. Using public finance, we illustrate that fiscal revenue will always be a small portion of economic impact thus, local revenues rarely exceed actual government expenses, and fiscal loss occurs. Furthermore, the extensive literature on sport events confirms they are regularly subject to high costs, overruns, and losses, nearly all of which must be borne by the public due to contractual obligations. Thus, government losses result in negative redistributive effects that harm local residents and benefit private industry. We propose dispensing with economic impact and using fiscal analysis as a tool to determine how sport subsidies can be provided at a level that offers the benefit of the public good but does not harm local residents through excessive spending, and thus, regressive redistribution.

title: Sanctions, and Subordinate Financialization: The Internal Spatial Fix in Iran
affiliations: State University of New York (SUNY) - Stony Brook, Students

detail.title: Sanctions, and Subordinate Financialization: The Internal Spatial Fix in Iran
detail.abstract: This article examines how sanctions and subordinate financialization have transformed Iran's economy over the past decade through the lens of the internal spatial fix. Constrained by global economic isolation, Iran has redirected financial capital from industrial manufacturing to speculative and extractive sectors, resulting in deindustrialization, heightened resource dependency, and a bifurcated labor regime marked by precarity and inequality. Adapting David Harvey's concept of the spatial fix to internal dynamics, this article situates Iran's trajectory within broader debates on financialization in peripheral economies, offering a novel lens to examine the interplay between sanctions, resource dependency, and economic precarity. Grounded in dissertation research, this article draws on two case studies-the decline of HEPCO and the rise of CMIC-to illustrate the mechanisms and consequences of this internal reallocation of capital. These findings reveal how sanctions and financialization intersect to prioritize short-term accumulation over long-term development, deepening economic instability and labor commodification. By integrating the overlapping effects of sanctions and financialization, this article offers a novel theoretical framework for understanding resource dependency and developmental stagnation in the Global South.

title: Demand for Basketball: A Comparison of the WNBA and NBA
affiliations: and Southern Utah University

detail.title: Demand for Basketball: A Comparison of the WNBA and NBA
detail.abstract: There is considerable discussion regarding interest in women's basketball, with critics often comparing the WNBA and NBA. This comparison is problematic because the WNBA is in an early growth phase while the NBA organizational life cycle position is far more mature. We investigate whether the demand features of early growth leagues are similar by comparing attendance data from the 8th-21st seasons of the WNBA with attendance from the same point in NBA history and the current NBA. We find the factors that affect demand in the WNBA are uniquely different than the NBA in both size and significance in either period, thus, it is inappropriate to compare the two leagues.

title: Digital Money and Payment Flow Competition
affiliations: University of Liverpool Management School, , Loyola Marymount University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Digital Money and Payment Flow Competition
detail.abstract: Traditional banks rely on informational synergy between payment and credit services: information from checking accounts helps them assess borrowers and thus issue credit. Non-bank digital money like Venmo disrupts this link by reducing banks' access to such information and unbundling payments from credit. We develop a New-Monetarist model with endogenous portfolio and banking choices under private information. When policy rates are high, buyers are less likely to use deposits to conceal information and extract rents; when rates are low, they are more likely to use deposits and reveal information. We show that non-bank digital money weakens informational synergy and intensifies bank disintermediation; however, credit allocation may improve, potentially raising welfare.

title: Advanced Machine Learning Methods for Churn Prediction and Classification in the Telecom Sector
affiliations: The Huntington National Bank

detail.title: Advanced Machine Learning Methods for Churn Prediction and Classification in the Telecom Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The telecom industry's vast client base causes it to create massive amounts of data daily. The cost of obtaining new clients is higher than the cost of keeping existing ones, according to business experts and decision-makers. Customer churn remains a critical challenge in the telecom sector, where retaining existing customers is significantly more cost-effective than acquiring new ones. This study focuses on applying advanced machine learning techniques to accurately predict and classify customer churn using the Telco Customer Churn dataset. The methodology includes comprehensive data preprocessing such as handling missing values, converting data types, encoding categorical features, scaling, and addressing class imbalance using SMOTE. The dataset is split into training and testing sets, and models including XGBoost, Extra Trees, and a Voting Classifier are developed and fine-tuned using Randomized SearchCV. Evaluation is conducted using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, confusion matrices, and classification reports. Among the models tested, the Extra Trees classifier achieved the highest performance with 86.05% accuracy, recall, and F1-score, outperforming both the Voting Classifier and XGBoost. Additionally, it surpassed baseline models like KNN, Logistic Regression, SGD, and Random Forest, and demonstrated more balanced performance compared to the stacking model, which, despite delivering competitive results, exhibited lower recall and less consistency across evaluation metrics. The results confirm that the Extra Trees model provides a robust and balanced solution for churn prediction, offering valuable insights for telecom providers in developing proactive customer retention strategies.

title: The Kedarnath Tragedy of 2013: Intersections of Natural Fury and Human Negligence in the Himalayan Region
affiliations: Kurukshetra University

detail.title: The Kedarnath Tragedy of 2013: Intersections of Natural Fury and Human Negligence in the Himalayan Region
detail.abstract: The Kedarnath disaster was one of India's most catastrophic natural events, intensified by a dangerous confluence of climate change, unregulated development, and institutional failures. Triggered by glacial lake outburst and record-breaking rainfall in the Garhwal Himalayas, the tragedy resulted in over 10000 deaths and extensive destruction of lives and infrastructure. This paper critically examines the socio-environmental and policy dimensions that magnified the disaster's impact. Drawing on secondary data, the study highlights how the convergence of fragile ecosystems, religious tourism, and governance failures led to a compounded disaster. A comparative analysis with the Chamoli, Leh, and Joshimath disasters further underscores systemic gaps in risk-sensitive planning. The Kedarnath tragedy serves as a stark reminder of the urgent need to strike a balance between development and environmental integrity in the Himalayan terrains. The question is 'Could the massive loss of life, property and environment have been avoided and, if so, to what extent? ' To answer these questions, this paper aims to carry out an objective Hazard, Vulnerability and Response Assessment of the State of Uttarakhand.

title: Skill-biased Technological Changes, Non-separable Utility, and Dynamic Optimal Capital Tax
affiliations: Zhejiang University and Zhejiang University - College of Economics

detail.title: Skill-biased Technological Changes, Non-separable Utility, and Dynamic Optimal Capital Tax
detail.abstract: This paper examines the optimal dynamic taxation of capital in the context of skill-biased technological changes. The study reveals that the widening wage gap, coupled with the complementarity between consumption and leisure, provides a novel rationale for capital taxation. It demonstrates that taxing capital is beneficial in economies experiencing persistent skillbiased technological advancements, even if the capital is skill-neutral and the complementarity between consumption and leisure is time invariant. Converse results appear when leisure substitutes consumption. Statistics-based optimal tax formulas are provided to show how the government can dynamically mitigate the impacts of various technological changes through the utilization of labor and capital income taxes.

title: Just Transition Pathways for a Net-Zero Telangana: Case Studies from Coal-Dependent Districts of Mancherial and Peddapalli
affiliations: Independent, Swaniti Initiative, Independent, Swaniti Initiative and Swaniti Initiative

detail.title: Just Transition Pathways for a Net-Zero Telangana: Case Studies from Coal-Dependent Districts of Mancherial and Peddapalli
detail.abstract: As the world moves towards a net zero future—a prerequisite for limiting the rise in average global temperatures to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels—coal phase down has become inevitable. India’s net zero target year is 2070. However, some coal-rich states like Telangana are setting an even more ambitious target of going net zero by 2047, that is, 23 years before the national target. As Telangana, which produces 7% of the total coal in India, actively plans its net-zero future, it seeks to ensure that workers and communities are protected from the aftereffects of coal phase down. To contribute to the understanding of Telangana’s net zero future and just transition prospects, we conducted a study to examine its current levels of coal dependence and economic diversification potential. For this, we focused on two key coal-dependent districts in Telangana: Mancherial and Peddapalli. Currently, these districts collectively produce 45% of the state's coal. Furthermore, these districts are home to several coal-based thermal power plants, fly ash units, and coal-dependent MSMEs. Notably, Ramagundam, located in Peddapalli district, stands out as a significant hub for thermal power generation in India. We conducted a mixed-methods study that included household and enterprise surveys in both districts to quantify coal dependence and unpack aspirations for understanding economic diversification. Additionally, we conducted multiple focus group discussions and semi-structured interviews to capture the nuanced realities, opportunities, and challenges related to diversification in these areas. Finally, we aligned our findings from field work with the existing policy landscape to identify potential support for new sectors.

reference: 52 Notre Dame Journal of Legislation ___ (forthcoming Spring 2026)
title: Genetic Parentage Acknowledgments: The Need for Congressional Action
affiliations: Northern Illinois University - College of Law

detail.title: Genetic Parentage Acknowledgments: The Need for Congressional Action

publicationDetails.detailsText: 52 Notre Dame Journal of Legislation ___ (forthcoming Spring 2026)

detail.abstract:
Genetic Parentage Acknowledgments: 

The Need for Congressional Action

52 Notre Dame Journal of Legislation ___ (forthcoming Spring 2026)

In the 1990s Congress, through the Social Security Act, required states receiving Title IV-D financial support to implement paternity acknowledgment processes. These processes are now generally utilized by states to designate (male genetic) paternity for children born of consensual sex regardless of any state financial assistance.

For states participating in the IV-D reimbursement program, Congress requires “fraud, duress, or material mistake of fact” as necessary for judicial overrides of paternity acknowledgments through signatory challenges brought more than sixty days after signing. Congress has not defined these terms, resulting in widespread variations in state laws. Congress also has not spoken on nonsignatory acknowledgment challenges.

Unfortunately, some state laws, again prompted by the 2017 UPA, have carried the fraud, duress and mistake challenge requirements over to parentage acknowledgments that are not based on actual or possible genetic ties. Signatory female spouses of gestating parents who acknowledge need not have provided eggs to prompt pregnancies and births. Signatory intended parents (male or female) who acknowledge need not be genetically tied to children born of nonsurrogacy assisted reproduction.  

The federal fraud, duress, and mistake norms on acknowledgment challenges do not necessarily apply to, and need not govern, challenges to acknowledgments that do not involve paternity or maternity based on possible genetic ties. Overrides of spousal parent acknowledgments, in the absence of actual or alleged genetic ties, should have separate challenge guidelines. Overrides of intended assisted reproduction parentage acknowledgments by those without actual or genetic ties should have separate challenge guidelines.  The 2017 UPA drafters could have recognized such differences in acknowledgment challenges, but did not.

One vehicle for prompting different acknowledgment challenge norms for the varied circumstances underlying acknowledgments is through Congressional amendments to the Social Security Act. Upon reviewing the current federal statutes and state laws on establishing and overriding all forms of parentage acknowledgments, the paper suggests Congressional actions that will better protect acknowledged children, acknowledging parents, nonsignatory genetic parents, and nonsignatory genetic and nongenetic family members who are related to acknowledged children.  

The paper urges Congress to recognize expressly the broad discretion held by state lawmakers regarding parentage acknowledgments beyond the scope of IV-D child support reimbursements from genetic parents. Within the IV-D realm, the paper urges Congress to revise its genetic acknowledgment requirements by promoting more uniform approaches to fraud, duress, and mistake. Express limits by Congress of IV-D acknowledgment norms to actual and alleged genetic parents would operate where social policies overwhelmingly support initial child support duties for genetic parents.

New federal norms guiding challenges to paternity acknowledgments for children born of consensual sex will need to differ from the norms guiding challenges to paternity/maternity acknowledgments for children born of assisted reproduction. Further, Congress should differentiate between nonsurrogacy, gestational surrogacy, and genetic surrogacy assisted reproduction births. Prebirth and/or postbirth parental childcare intentions should generally operate for children born of sex while preconception parental childcare intentions should usually operate for assisted reproduction birth children.

The paper also suggests that Congress consider expanding its IV-D parentage establishment mandates, aimed at increasing reimbursements to governments for welfare payments, to include nongenetic (both custodial and noncustodial) parents who are recognized under state laws as childcare (i.e., custody and support) parents. Where state laws place on equal footing, for example, genetic parents and nongenetic de facto parents for child custody purposes, all such parents should be comparably treated for child support reimbursement purposes.

title: Institutional Design of Asymmetric Decentralization for Conflict Mitigation: Learning from the ARMM-BARMM Transition
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy

detail.title: Institutional Design of Asymmetric Decentralization for Conflict Mitigation: Learning from the ARMM-BARMM Transition
detail.abstract: Territorial autonomy is frequently promoted as a solution to ethnic conflict, yet its outcomes vary widely across cases. This paper argues that asymmetric decentralization succeeds in mitigating ethnic conflict only when its institutional design demonstrates coherence, context-sensitivity, and alignment with the underlying structure of conflict grievances. Drawing on recent research showing that institutional design quality determines the effectiveness of asymmetric arrangements, the study develops a threepillar framework emphasizing: (1) fiscal-legal integration that ensures both autonomy and accountability through automatic transfers and constitutional entrenchment; (2) inclusive governance architecture that accommodates competing elites while maintaining democratic representativeness; and (3) adaptive coordination systems that manage intergovernmental relations while preserving flexibility for institutional evolution. The framework is illustrated through a comparative analysis of the Philippines' transition from the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) to the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM)-a rare case of comprehensive asymmetric redesign within constant territorial and constitutional conditions. The study finds that ARMM failed due to fiscal dependency, exclusionary politics, weak legal entrenchment, and absence of coordination mechanisms. In contrast, BARMM introduced automatic block grants, parliamentary governance, formal elite integration, enhanced cultural autonomy, and systematic intergovernmental relations bodies-each mapped to address the multi-dimensional grievances of the Moro conflict. The analysis reveals that asymmetric arrangements' effectiveness depends not on formal power allocation but on institutional design coherence and conflict-structure alignment. While acknowledging BARMM's recent establishment limits definitive outcome assessment, early evidence suggests promising institutional developments including improved public satisfaction, increased service delivery, and enhanced fiscal autonomy. The paper contributes to federal design theory by providing the first systematic framework linking ethnic conflict typologies to asymmetric institutional design, and demonstrates that failed arrangements can be successfully redesigned through institutional learning and stakeholder inclusion.

title: Speed, Style Status: Cultural and Economic Impact of Ferrari and Fiat on Italian Consumer Identity (1945 -1985)
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Speed, Style Status: Cultural and Economic Impact of Ferrari and Fiat on Italian Consumer Identity (1945 -1985)
detail.abstract: Post World War 2 Italy had faced economic collapse, widespread poverty, high unemployment rates and a fractured national identity. This paper examines how two contrasting automotive manufacturers, Fiat and Ferrari, played complementary roles in rebuilding Italy's economy and identity between 1945 and 1985. Fiat, under Vittorio Valletta, contributed to Italy's postwar economic recovery through large-scale production and labor absorption and Ferrari contributed with technological innovation, motorsport and export visibility while under Enzo Ferrari. Even though they differed in audiences and production ideologies both brands were monumental in redefining Italian modernity. Using economic data, Marshall plan recovery reports, labor and gender documents, and advertising campaigns, this paper will explore how both automotive giants not only responded to Italy's postwar crisis but also actively shaped consumer psychology, industrial growth and class identity. By integrating cultural, economic, and legal analysis, this study demonstrates that Italy's recovery was driven as much by symbolism and consumer aspiration as by fiscal policy or infrastructure.

reference: Journal of Sports Economics, volume 25, issue 6, 2024[10.1177/15270025241260030]
title: The Effect of National Origin and Skin Color on Playing Time in the WNBA
affiliations: , Southern Utah University and Ursinus College

detail.title: The Effect of National Origin and Skin Color on Playing Time in the WNBA

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Sports Economics, volume 25, issue 6, 2024[10.1177/15270025241260030]

detail.abstract: This article uses data from the 1997-2022 seasons to investigate the role of bias in the distribution of playing time in the WNBA. We evaluate national origin, a fixed and objective measure, and improve upon past uses of subjective, perception-based measures of race by using a more objective measure of skin tone. More specifically, via a fixed-effect estimation of 2,949 WNBA player-year combinations we find no evidence that the national origin of either players or coaches is related to the provision of playing time. Similarly, skin tone of players or coaches (n=893), either alone or in combination with national origin, shows no robust significance. Evidence of national origin bias has previously been reported in professional men's basketball leagues in the U.S., Spain, and China. The WNBA may be demographically similar to the NBA, but it is culturally different and we find no evidence of employer discrimination.

title: Ethereum's Role in the US Government's New Stablecoin Architecture: A detailed analysis of Regulatory, Technical, and Economic Implications
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Ethereum's Role in the US Government's New Stablecoin Architecture: A detailed analysis of Regulatory, Technical, and Economic Implications
detail.abstract: The United States has established the world's first comprehensive federal regulatory framework for stablecoins through the GENIUS Act, signed into law on July 18, 2025. This landmark legislation creates a structured environment for digital dollar infrastructure, with Ethereum blockchain hosting approximately 70% of the global stablecoin supply exceeding $200 billion. This research examines Ethereum's multifaceted role within this new regulatory architecture, analyzing technical capabilities, economic impacts, compliance considerations, and competitive positioning. The study reveals that while Ethereum maintains dominance through network effects and institutional trust, scalability challenges and emerging competition from alternative blockchains create strategic pressures. The research demonstrates that Ethereum-based stablecoins offer significant economic benefits including reduced transaction costs and enhanced financial inclusion, while also presenting systemic risks requiring careful regulatory oversight. The analysis concludes that a multi-platform ecosystem is emerging, with Ethereum likely maintaining leadership through continued dominance in decentralized finance infrastructure and institutional adoption.

title: Sustainable Cities : Interdisciplinary Perspective
affiliations: Environment Europe Foundation

detail.title: Sustainable Cities : Interdisciplinary Perspective
detail.abstract: This chapter explores the problem of integrated interdisciplinary research in the fi eld of sustainable cities. The problematique of urban sustainability is studied in its historical and international context. Current research in the fi eld is reviewed, and major gaps in interdisciplinary analysis are identifi ed. This chapter makes fi rst steps towards the development of an innovative methodology for the analysis of interdisciplinary links between various sustainability dimensions in the urban context. The dimensions taken into consideration are: sustainable energy, sustainable transport, material fl ows and waste management, quality of life, health, psychology of interaction with the environment, green space, biodiversity, preservation of the natural and cultural heritage, landscape architecture, ecodesign and democratic participation. Two great European cities, London and St Petersburg, are analysed from the point of view of integrative policies and instruments applied in the fi eld of sustainable urban development. The two cities are compared using a panel of sustainability indicators.

title: Canada's Digital Asset Opportunity: Shaping a Strategic Path to Global Leadership
affiliations: Ivey Business School and University of Western Ontario - Ivey Business School

detail.title: Canada's Digital Asset Opportunity: Shaping a Strategic Path to Global Leadership

declarations.funderStatement: This work was produced in collaboration with Ivey’s Scotiabank Digital Banking Lab. We gratefully acknowledge the generous support of the Lawrence Family, the Baran Family Foundation, the Canada Life Research Fund, the Power Corporation of Canada, and Scotiabank.

detail.abstract:
In collaboration with the Scotiabank Digital Banking Lab, the LNC presents a new perspective policy brief: Canada’s Digital Asset Opportunity: Shaping a Strategic Path to Global Leadership. Authored by Hubert Pun and Amin Mazhari (PhD ’27), the brief explores how Canada is at a pivotal moment in the evolution of the digital economy. Blockchain technologies, digital assets, and tokenized financial systems are no longer emerging trends. They are rapidly becoming part of the core infrastructure for financial innovation, inclusion, and economic competitiveness. 

Canada holds strong foundations: respected regulatory institutions, world-class talent, and a history of early exploration in blockchain research and digital identity frameworks. However, the global race for digital asset leadership is accelerating. Countries such as the United States (through the FIT Act), the European Union (via MiCA), Japan, Singapore, and the UAE are implementing comprehensive frameworks that enable secure stablecoins, digital asset custody, and open financial innovation ecosystems. Meanwhile, Canada risks falling behind. The absence of a coordinated national strategy, limited banking access for blockchain-based firms, and regulatory uncertainty push talent and capital abroad, stifling innovation and undermining long-term competitiveness in financial services and digital infrastructure. 

This brief outlines an actionable roadmap for Canada to reclaim its leadership and secure its position in the programmable economy. With the right strategy, Canada can foster a trusted and competitive digital economy, stimulate high-quality jobs, and deliver long-term economic growth. But without urgent and collaborative action, it risks becoming a follower in an increasingly digital global financial order.

title: A Key Sector Approach to the Environmentally Extended Input-Output Analysis of the UK Economy
affiliations: Environment Europe Foundation

detail.title: A Key Sector Approach to the Environmentally Extended Input-Output Analysis of the UK Economy
detail.abstract: This chapter is devoted to the application of a novel interdisciplinary method based on combining environmentally-extended input-output analysis with MCDA

title: If I Ruled the World: Power, Profit, and the Commodification of Mental Health: How Pharma, Private Equity, and Policy Capitalize on America’s Mental Health Crisis
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: If I Ruled the World: Power, Profit, and the Commodification of Mental Health: How Pharma, Private Equity, and Policy Capitalize on America’s Mental Health Crisis
detail.abstract: The United States finds itself at a paradoxical juncture where mental health and addiction have transformed into both a public crisis and a private market (Zeira, 2021). This paper interrogates how the rhetoric of “empathy” and “compassionate care” conceals a deeper truth: the commodification of mental health as a vehicle for profit and power (Sousa et al., 2022). While policymakers tout increased funding for suicide prevention, addiction treatment, and crisis response, the underlying beneficiaries are not the communities most at risk but the pharmaceutical giants, private equity firms, and billionaire investors who position themselves at the back end of federal funding pipelines. Urban America only presents a partial picture. Cities such as Memphis, Detroit, Baltimore, and St. Louis are repeatedly labeled as “most dangerous” due to violent crime, yet the conditions fueling this violence—concentrated poverty, racial segregation, underfunded schools, and systemic neglect remain unaddressed (Zhang et al., 2020). Meanwhile, in rural America, the crisis takes a different form: suicide, addiction, and domestic violence (Houlihan & Williamson, 2023). West Virginia, Appalachia, and struggling Midwestern towns experience staggering rates of overdose deaths and untreated trauma, framed in policy circles as a “mental health emergency.” However, rather than tackling structural inequalities, political leaders redirect suffering into individualized treatment models that are financially lucrative but socially shallow. What appears to be an outpouring of empathy for mental health is, in fact, a carefully constructed power grab. By medicalizing social despair, billionaires and private equity firms profit from treatment centers, luxury rehab “resorts,” and pharmaceutical interventions, while rights-based protections for women, LGBTQ communities, and people of color are simultaneously defunded. Mental health becomes the bipartisan “safe issue” that both avoids cultural war controversies and generates enormous corporate profit. This paper argues that America’s mental health funding surge is less a reflection of genuine compassion and more a political economy of suffering where despair is monetized, trauma is outsourced to private markets, and systemic injustice is left intact. The crisis, both urban and rural, becomes a financial opportunity, ensuring that the very communities most harmed remain trapped in cycles of violence, poverty, and unaddressed inequality.

title: Promotion Design under Dual Reputation Concerns: Substitutes or Complements?
affiliations: Washington University in St-Louis and Nihon University - College of Economics

detail.title: Promotion Design under Dual Reputation Concerns: Substitutes or Complements?
detail.abstract: We study optimal promotion design when observed success pools two latent fundamentals: managerial ability and task ease. We build a two-period career-concerns model in which project success depends on ability, ease, and observable effort, while the firm commits to an outcome-contingent promotion rule and a continuation decision. The key object is the posterior dispersion of the promoted worker's ability ("reputational volatility"). We show that its comparative statics with respect to first-period success are pinned down by the technology's modularity: under submodularity (ability and ease are substitutes), success lowers reputational volatility; under supermodularity (complements), it raises it. With convex utility over reputation, the optimal rule inverts the usual logic: the firm promotes after failure under substitutability and after success under complementarity. The continuation decision co-moves: promotion may be paired with termination even when continuation is profitable in expectation under supermodularity, and conversely, the firm may continue projects with negative expected profits to preserve reputational option value under submodularity.

title: Blood in the Name of Belief: Mob Violence and Minority Targeting in India
affiliations: Kurukshetra University

detail.title: Blood in the Name of Belief: Mob Violence and Minority Targeting in India
detail.abstract: Mob lynching in India is not a new deviance but a deeply rooted phenomenon with historical origins going back to the Partition period. This paper critically examines its genesis, main causes, and long-term influence on the social fabric. Social media has immensely fuelled such violence, facilitating the instant dissemination of misinformation and fuelling mass vigilantism. Political discourse, ingrained societal biases, and profound religious prejudices tend to sanction these acts within particular socio-political environments. Ineffective legislation and lax government reactions further complicate the situation. Focusing on iconic incidents like the Dadri and Alwar lynching (2015-2018), the research highlights the manner in which mob violence shakes up communities and represents serious breaches of human rights. It spots significant legal and institutional loopholes and calls for comprehensive reforms ranging from stringent anti-lynching laws, increased political accountability, and sustained educational programs to combat hate violence and build communal peace across India.

title: An Assessment of the Financial Sustainability and Performance of Philippine Water Districts
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy

detail.title: An Assessment of the Financial Sustainability and Performance of Philippine Water Districts
detail.abstract: This study evaluates the consolidated financial condition and performance of local water districts (LWDs) in the Philippines. Water districts are government-owned or controlled corporations (GOCCs) tasked to construct, operate, maintain, and expand water and sanitation systems in the countryside. They are instrumental in the Philippines' objective to attain 100-percent water supply and sanitation access by 2036. National data show that the consolidated financial performance of LWDs has improved from 2009 to 2018, as reflected in their high and stable cash flows, high debt service coverage ratios, and lower debt ratios. With the aggressive spending program of the government on water infrastructure, lower debt ratios are needed to prepare LWDs to achieve the 2023 and the 2030 goals of universal access to water supply and sanitation. However, the government's spending plans are so ambitious that the current balance sheets of LWDs cannot sustain the planned investments financed through debt. The national government needs to bolster the balance sheets of LWDs by infusing fresh equity of PHP 22 billion to PHP 56 billion to achieve the Philippines' 2030 water supply and sanitation targets. The study likewise shows a significant disparity in water investments across the country's different regions, which impacts the uneven water service coverage throughout the Philippines.

title: Rhythmic Expression Rights （RER）｜A Process-Based Copyright Layer for Human–AI Co-Creation：A Next-Generation Framework for Protecting Structural and Rhythmic Expression
affiliations: The University of Manchester

detail.title: Rhythmic Expression Rights （RER）｜A Process-Based Copyright Layer for Human–AI Co-Creation：A Next-Generation Framework for Protecting Structural and Rhythmic Expression
detail.abstract: Generative AI produces vast outputs by imitating and recombining prior works’ structural–rhythmic patterns (SRP)—the modular structures, temporal cadences, and collaboration pathways that organize expression. Traditional copyright, optimized for finished artifacts, under-protects these process-level features and struggles to allocate credit and liability in multi-party human–AI workflows. This paper proposes Rhythmic Expression Rights (RER), a complementary rights layer that attaches to how expression is organized and sequenced rather than only what is said or shown. We formalize RER’s protected subject matter (SRP), articulate a bundle of rights (attribution, licensing/remuneration, control, traceability, anti-passing-off), and set fair-use boundaries (idea/expression split, independent creation, minimal interoperability, educational exceptions). To render RER justiciable, we introduce an evidence model built on the SER × CSL × Rhythm OS stack: machine-generated structure logs, rhythmic fingerprints, timestamping, and multi-party signatures that make “process = provenance.” We provide a minimal viable implementation for platforms and studios, cross-modal applicability (text, music, video, code), privacy-preserving verification (including zero-knowledge proofs), and a governance pathway spanning platform terms, industry registries, and legal adoption.Case analyses show how RER addresses “new skin, same skeleton” replication and enables auditable, contribution-weighted revenue sharing. We argue RER is protocol-grade: non-proprietary, interoperable, and capable of lowering transaction costs across jurisdictions. The result is a pragmatic legal-technical substrate for human–AI co-creation—shifting the center of gravity from post-hoc content similarity to verifiable creative process and establishing an actionable framework for attribution, licensing, and compliance in the age of AI.

title: Litigation As Collective Action Strategy a Political-Legal Perspective on Public-Interest Litigation
affiliations: Leiden University and

detail.title: Litigation As Collective Action Strategy a Political-Legal Perspective on Public-Interest Litigation
detail.abstract: When do civil society organizations initiate legal proceedings against their government? Public interest litigation has a long history and rich research tradition in the United States. With this paper we aim to contribute to the recently emerging European literature on strategic litigation strategies of civil society organizations beyond the US system. To do so, we combine the literatures of litigation strategies and interest representation to explain the prevalence of strategic litigation. In a case study of the Netherlands, we draw on a combination of a legal analysis and unique survey data of political activities by Dutch civil society organizations. This paper thereby offers a political-legal perspective on the practice of pursuing lawsuits as collective action strategy in a European context. Our findings suggest that strategic litigation is an emerging, highly contextualized phenomenon with important implications for both interest representation and for the relations between legislative and judicial branches in democratic systems.

title: Exchange Rate Fluctuations and Nigeria's Economic Growth: SVAR Impact Investigation
affiliations: Federal Polytechnic, Bali, Taraba State, Bayero University and Taraba State University

detail.title: Exchange Rate Fluctuations and Nigeria's Economic Growth: SVAR Impact Investigation
detail.abstract: The research examines exchange rate fluctuations on Nigeria`s economic growth in order to get a deeper understanding of the relationship, four macroeconomic variables real GDP (RGDP), nominal exchanges rate (NXR), inflation (INF), and interest rate (INT) were chosen. Annual series data was used covering a period of 42 years. The overall interpretation of the SVAR model's results indicates that Nigeria's economic growth is positively impacted by the nominal rate of exchange (0.638), despite this relationship is statistically not significant. In addition, there is a sharply negative correlation between Nigeria's economic growth and the country's interest rate (-4.065) and inflation rate (-0.063). The research suggests that fixed exchange rates should be preferred for smaller economies such as Nigeria. The Nigerian CBN has to integrate its exchange rate policies with other economic objectives, such as the control of inflation.

title: Competitiveness of Uzbekistan's Agri-Food Exports
affiliations: Sumgait State University and Bağımsız Araştırmacı

detail.title: Competitiveness of Uzbekistan's Agri-Food Exports
detail.abstract: The article analyzes the export performance of Uzbekistan's fruit and vegetable products and evaluates their competitiveness in the global market using practical index-based methods. The analysis is based on data from the International Trade Centre, and 12 products classified under the HS-4 code were selected for the study. The Trade Balance Index was used to determine whether the country is a net exporter or importer of these products. Competitiveness in exports was assessed using the Balassa and Vollrath indices. The analysis revealed that 9 out of the 12 products are competitive, and Uzbekistan acts as a net exporter of these goods. The findings highlight the need for the country to diversify its export basket and expand into new international markets.

title: Never Too Late: Apprenticeship Training Late in The Career as a Way Out of Age Discrimination
affiliations: Ghent University, Ghent University, Ghent University and Hogeschool-Universiteit Brussel (HUBrussel)

detail.title: Never Too Late: Apprenticeship Training Late in The Career as a Way Out of Age Discrimination
detail.abstract: In many countries, age discrimination appears to be driven by negative perceptions that recruiters stereotypically hold about older candidates' technological skills, trainability, and flexibility. Based on multiple theories, we hypothesise that training programmes might mitigate these ageist stereotypes and thereby improve these candidates' recruitability. We test this pathway out of age discrimination by designing a vignette experiment in which professional recruiters assess the recruitability and human capital perceptions of fictitious candidates varying in age and (willingness for) participation in apprenticeship training at older ages. Our results demonstrate that candidates indicating their (willingness for) participation in such training to obtain relevant work experience are more likely to be recruited than candidates without such experience, regardless of their age. Moreover, recent participation also mitigates age discrimination, as the premium it yields is higher for candidates aged 55 and older. Nevertheless, no robust differences in perceptions are observed.

title: When Tails Are Heavy: The Benefits of Variance-Targeted, Non-Gaussian, Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation of GARCH Models 1
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: When Tails Are Heavy: The Benefits of Variance-Targeted, Non-Gaussian, Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation of GARCH Models 1
detail.abstract: In heavy-tailed cases, variance targeting the Student's-t estimator proposed in Bollerslev (1987) for the linear GARCH model is shown to be robust to density misspecification, just like the popular Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimator (QMLE). The resulting Variance-Targeted, Non-Gaussian, Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimator (VTNGQMLE) is shown to possess a stable limit, albeit one that is highly non-Gaussian, with an ill-defined variance. The rate of convergence to this non-standard limit is slow relative to root-n and dependent upon unknown parameters. Fortunately, the sub-sample bootstrap is applicable, given a carefully constructed normalization. Surprisingly, both Monte Carlo experiments and empirical applications reveal VTNGQMLE to sizably outperform QMLE and other performance-enhancing (relative to QMLE) alternatives. In an empirical application, VTNGQMLE is applied to VIX (option-implied volatility of the S&P 500 Index). The resulting GARCH variance estimates are then used to forecast option-implied volatility of volatility (VVIX), thus demonstrating a link between historical volatility of VIX and risk-neutral volatility-of-volatility.

title: When Private Firms Provide Public Goods: The Allocation of CSR Spending
affiliations: LSE Finance Department, Queen Mary University of London and Columbia University in the City of New York

detail.title: When Private Firms Provide Public Goods: The Allocation of CSR Spending
detail.abstract: This paper studies how firms allocate their Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) expenditures to inform the welfare effects of corporate contributions to public goods. Using a novel dataset containing detailed information on the quasi-universe of firms' CSR projects in India over the period 2015-2019, we document key facts on the allocation of CSR spending across social topics (e.g., health, education) and locations. We develop a new method to measure the technological proximity between firms' production technology and CSR topics using natural language processing, and find that firms spend more on topics in which they have a technological advantage. This is consistent with an efficient allocation of CSR expenditures across topics and the main rationale for CSR in the literature. Considering allocation across locations, however, we find that firms spend more in areas where social returns are likely lower. Overall, our results suggest that CSR mandates may be an efficient but inequitable way to increase public goods provision.

title: Balance-Sheet Netting in U.S. Treasury Markets and Central Clearing
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Balance-Sheet Netting in U.S. Treasury Markets and Central Clearing
detail.abstract: This paper examines the potential for expanded central clearing to reduce the costs of the supplementary leverage ratio (SLR) on Treasury market intermediation. Using unique regulatory data, we find that the SEC's new rules on central clearing would have limited effects on SLR levels, even during the March 2020 turmoil. We first clarify that central clearing does not impact balance sheet netting for Treasury cash transactions. For repos, significant activity remains non-nettable even if centrally cleared, while substantial netting already occurs bilaterally. We also explore banks' balance sheet netting optimization incentives, contributing valuable perspectives to Treasury market structure debates.

title: Geographic Disparities in Medicare Esketamine (Spravato) Access: A Claims-Based Analysis Documenting a 24-State Treatment Desert (September 2025)

detail.title: Geographic Disparities in Medicare Esketamine (Spravato) Access: A Claims-Based Analysis Documenting a 24-State Treatment Desert (September 2025)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: In 2023, Medicare Fee-for-Service (FFS) clinic-billed esketamine (Spravato) appears in only 26 states; 24 states report zero clinic-billed use. Despite this geographic void, clinic-billed volume rose ~60% year-over-year (14,290 → 22,917 services; ≈$20.8M paid). National Part B totals-which also include hospital-outpatient settings that CMS does not publish by state-are 25,532 services and ≈$22.37M paid in 2023 (rising to 38,240 and ≈$34.18M in 2024), a ~10% uplift over the clinic-only state sum.

title: The Impact of International Sanctions on Russia’s Energy Sector
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Impact of International Sanctions on Russia’s Energy Sector
detail.abstract:
In recent years, there has been an aggravation of the geopolitical situation in the world, while the beginning of Russia's special military operation in Ukraine (SVO) was a critical point, after which the situation deteriorated significantly. Its impact has caused a negative reaction from developed countries, primarily the United States and the EU, which has had a significant impact on all sectors of the economy, including the energy sector. At the same time, the oil and gas sector is one of the most important sectors for the Russian economy, since, according to Rosstat, it accounted for 17.4% of Russia's GDP in 2021 (in 2020, this figure was 13.9%). Thus, Russia's dependence on oil and gas revenues is significant and tends to increase when comparing the figures for 2021 and 2020. This is confirmed by the data of the Accounting Chamber, according to which in 2021 oil and gas revenues accounted for 34.5% of federal budget revenues.

Today, the global energy sector is undergoing a strong transformation, and the issue of energy security is acute for countries.

The energy sector in Russia is one of the most important components of the country's economic development, its political power and the stability of the social sphere. In international relations, energy plays no less a significant role than the military might of the state. The state of the fuel and energy sector has a direct impact on such a component of the national security of the state as its energy security.

Due to the importance of the energy sector for the state's economy, energy diplomacy is of particular importance, the effective implementation of which allows the country to defend its interests and positions in the global energy market and in international energy relations. At the present stage, the effectiveness of Russia's energy diplomacy and its ability to defend Russia's interests in the energy sector against developed countries seeking to undermine Russia's position on the world stage in various ways, including through the imposition of sanctions, restrictions on the size of its oil and gas revenues, energy exports and the maximum possible ceiling on energy prices, largely depends on ensuring national security of the country.

In the spring of 2022, due to Russia's launch of a special military operation in Ukraine, a number of countries imposed a number of new sanctions against Russia. As a result, the states that joined the sanctions against Russia gradually began to abandon oil imports from Russia. The first Western country to impose an embargo on oil imports from Russia was Canada, which announced its introduction at the end of February 2022. However, such a decision by the Canadian authorities

had no impact on energy relations between Russia and Canada, as Canada has not imported crude oil from Russia since 2019.

title: Being Innovative or Being on the Safe Side -Managing the Risk of Failure
affiliations: National Research University Higher School of Economics (Moscow), affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Tsinghua University - School of Public Policy and Management, Tsinghua University and Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) - School of Applied Sciences

detail.title: Being Innovative or Being on the Safe Side -Managing the Risk of Failure
detail.abstract:
Innovation has long been at the center of debates in economics, management, and organizational studies. However, innovation is never free of uncertainty and risk. Every act of innovation implies a departure from established paths and a willingness to embrace the unknown. From the beginning it's never clear if there is an audience which appreciates the innovation. This inherent exposure to uncertainty gives rise to the central dilemma of this collection: whether to be innovative or to play it safe, and how to manage the inevitable risk of failure. The ways in which organizations and societies face this dilemma are profoundly shaped by culture. Cultural values and institutional norms determine how risk is perceived, how uncertainty is tolerated, and how failure is interpreted. Failure, in particular, is at the heart of this discussion. It can be understood as both a barrier and an opportunity.

Beyond cultural meanings and institutional incentives, risk itself emerges as a multifaceted phenomenon. It involves measurable probabilities and uncertainties, as well as narratives of trust, legitimacy, and responsibility. This interplay between ambition and prudence highlights the importance of striking a balance. Innovation cannot advance if all risks are avoided, but reckless exposure to uncertainty can threaten the very foundations of organizational and social stability. This collection seeks to explore these dilemmas by bringing together diverse and complementary perspectives. The volumedemonstrates, how organizational cultures shape behavior in the face of uncertainty, and how societies seek to balance ambition and responsibility. Altogether, the Work underscores the journey from culture to balance: beginning with the cultural foundations of risk-taking, moving through the mechanisms that reward experimentation, addressing the strategic problem of defining acceptable levels of risk, and culminating in the societal task of punishing innovation with safety.

title: Devalued Currencies and the Subsistence of Homeless People in Colombia
affiliations: EDUKIVOTOS

detail.title: Devalued Currencies and the Subsistence of Homeless People in Colombia
detail.abstract: This article analyzes the paradox between the low-denomination coins in circulation in Colombia (50, 100, 200, 500, and 1,000 pesos) and the accumulated inflation of more than two decades, which has profoundly deteriorated their purchasing power. Homeless people, who survive mainly by begging for coins in urban spaces, face an increasingly precarious situation: acts of symbolic solidarity are disconnected from the real ability to guarantee food, healthcare, or housing. From an interdisciplinary perspective, combining economics, sociology, and human rights, this work explores how the rigidity of nominal values, inflationary erosion, and the absence of public policies perpetuate exclusion, indignity, and extreme poverty. It raises the need for structural policies in line with the Sustainable Development Goals to protect the rights of the most vulnerable.

title: Bitcoin worlds
affiliations: Satoshi Action Education

detail.title: Bitcoin worlds

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Murray A Rudd reports a relationship with Satoshi Action Education, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, that includes: consulting or advisory.
declarations.funderStatement: This project received no funding.

detail.abstract: Bitcoin confronts the global monetary order with an unprecedented experiment of absolute scarcity in a system built on elastic credit. This paper develops a structured scenario framework to map 64 possible "Bitcoin worlds" defined by six institutional cleavages: liquidity depth, policy clarity, concentration of holdings, macro-energy stress, trust and information integrity, and credit leverage. Of these, 40 configurations appear to be internally coherent, while 24 are likely transitional states prone to breakdown. The analysis compares how Keynesian, Post-Keynesian, Austrian, and both Old and New Institutional Economics interprets Bitcoin's role, highlighting divergent views of stabilization, scarcity, and governance. Two worldviews dominate: one sovereignty-first in orientation, where resilience derives from decentralization, transparency, and grassroots practice; and a second stability-first worldview, where resilience stems from institutional scaffolding, deep liquidity, and regulatory integration. Leverage emerges as the modal divider between stability and fragility, and regional variation shapes paths toward custodial or decentralized worlds. By making priors explicit and trade-offs visible, the framework suggest that Bitcoin's trajectory will be set less by protocol rules than by governance choices, with implications for fiscal capacity, unit-of-account primacy, and the distribution of monetary authority.

title: The Original Function Of Tax Apportionment
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - School of Law and Washington University in St. Louis - School of Law

detail.title: The Original Function Of Tax Apportionment
detail.abstract:
The Constitution’s requirement that direct taxes be apportioned by state population is both confounding and important. At best, tax apportionment is regarded as reflecting the unique federalism concerns of the Founding; at worst, it is viewed as a tainted product of the constitutional compromise over slavery. And, in light of the Supreme Court’s decision in Moore v. United States (2024)—which refused to rule out that apportionment might be required for taxes on unrealized gains—tax apportionment is the subject of renewed legal and scholarly interest.

We consider one historical dimension of tax apportionment that has not been developed elsewhere: its original function. Today, apportionment can feel puzzling. But it emerged and persisted across hundreds of years of English, British, and American colonial practice because it was useful. We argue that the original function of tax apportionment was to solve a set of incentive problems that emerges when a central authority (like the crown) must rely on local authorities (like town and county officials) for tax gathering. In the context of this principal-agent problem, apportionment preserves the benefits of local flexibility—the local community can raise its allotment however it sees fit—but imposes a quota that limits flexibility and protects the central fisc. But we do not offer this theory to rationalize apportionment today. Indeed, understanding the original function of tax apportionment helps us understand exactly how far the Constitution’s use of tax apportionment strayed from its original purpose.

title: The Causal Impact of Education on Eudaimonic Wellbeing among Older Adults: Evidence from Europe
affiliations: University of South Australia and Flinders University

detail.title: The Causal Impact of Education on Eudaimonic Wellbeing among Older Adults: Evidence from Europe
detail.abstract: The purpose of this article is to examine the relationship between education and eudaimonic wellbeing among older adults. We draw on Waves 2-9 (2006-2022) of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). A Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) model is employed, using compulsory schooling as an instrument for completed years of education to address endogeneity concerns. The IV estimates indicate that an additional year of education raises eudaimonic wellbeing by 0.057 points on a 1-4 scale (p<0.01). Gender-specific estimates are similarly positive and significant: 0.054 for men and 0.060 for women (all p<0.01). By exploiting cross-national institutional variation and applying an instrumental variable strategy, this study provides one of the first robust causal estimates of how education promotes deeper dimensions of psychological functioning, beyond traditional health metrics, among older European adults.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Workplace Misconduct
affiliations: University of Bristol, University of Essex - Essex Business School and University of Exeter Business School

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Workplace Misconduct
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption on workplace misconduct. We combine firm-level data on financials, corporate governance, and workplace misconduct with a measure of AI adoption based on employees' AI-related skills. To identify causal effects, we exploit the 2015 release of Google TensorFlow as a plausibly exogenous shock within a difference-in-differences framework. We find that firms with higher pre-treatment AI intensity experience significant and persistent declines in workplace violations and penalty amounts after 2015. The effects operate primarily through productivity-enhancing complementarities, while labor-adjustment channels play no role. Benefits are concentrated among larger, intangible-and organizational-capital-intensive firms, which highlights uneven gains from AI adoption.

title: What Happens when Some Agents Over-Demand in Claims Problems
affiliations: Universitat de Barcelona, University of Barcelona - Department of Actuarial, Financial and Economic Mathematics and Universitat de Barcelona

detail.title: What Happens when Some Agents Over-Demand in Claims Problems
detail.abstract: In claims problems, we explore three characterizations of the constrained equal awards rule based on how allocations respond to an agent increasing its claim. In the first one we ensure that over-demanding by an unsatisfied agent does not harm others. In the second one we require that such over-demanding leaves the entire allocation unchanged. Finally, in the third one we weaken this last condition by protecting only the initially fully compensated agents.

title: Monitoring and Corruption in Networks

detail.title: Monitoring and Corruption in Networks
detail.abstract: I study how network structure affects the provision of public goods in the context of peer monitoring and corruption. Peer monitoring is modeled as network monitoring, where individuals observe only their neighbors' contributions perfectly and do not observe contributions of others. Corruption is captured by bribes individuals can pay their neighbors privately. I find that although corruption makes it easier for agents to shirk, it does not necessarily lead to zero contributions. I characterize the network structure for which full (and zero) contribution is the unique equilibrium outcome. Generally, I show existence of Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium in pure-strategies, and moreover, a unique outcome result for every connected network. This allows me to order network structures in aggregate contributions (the outcome). I exploit this feature to discuss agents' welfare, and optimal network design.

title: Macroeconomy: Market Failures and Externalities: What Can Be Done
affiliations: Environment Europe Foundation

detail.title: Macroeconomy: Market Failures and Externalities: What Can Be Done
detail.abstract: The concept of market failure has become central in defi ning the place, scope and effectiveness of government intervention in case of environmental pollution. This chapter presents the classic model of externalities and explains why current economic theories have not been very successful in fully tackling them. The concept of an environmental tax, designed in the spirit of the Arthur Pigou tax is introduced. Comparative analysis of various environmental taxes in major EU countries is made. The concept of an environmental tax is illustrated with the example of a landfi ll tax in two EU Member States: Austria and the Netherlands. It can be seen how different rates of environmental tax and the pace of their introduction could affect the development pattern of a municipal waste management system.

title: The Legacy of Growing Up in a Recession on Attitudes Towards European Union
affiliations: University of Macedonia and University of Luxembourg

detail.title: The Legacy of Growing Up in a Recession on Attitudes Towards European Union

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: In an era marked by repeated crises and the growing traction of populist movements, understanding the deep-rooted factors shaping EU cohesion has become increasingly urgent. This paper investigates how lifetime exposure to economic recessions influences individual attitudes toward the European Union (EU). Resorting to rich micro-data from the European Social Survey (ESS) and the Eurobarometer, we construct a detailed measure of economic hardship experienced during lifetime, capturing not just isolated downturns but the accumulated burden of multiple recessions over time. Importantly, we distinguish between various types of shocks-including output contractions, unemployment surges, consumption drops, participation in IMF adjustment programs, and the asymmetry or symmetry of crises across EU member states. We show that individuals with greater lifetime exposure to these economic shocks are more likely to distrust EU institutions, oppose further integration, vote for Eurosceptic parties, and support exiting the EU. These patterns are especially pronounced for asymmetric shocks, which disproportionately affect specific regions or countries, in contrast to symmetric shocks, which appear to foster a sense of shared fate and solidarity. A series of robustness tests-including placebo checks, heterogeneity analyses, diverse shock types and designs exploiting EU institutional structure -confirms the persistent impact of economic trauma on EU attitudes, underscoring the need to address historical recessions to safeguard cohesion and democratic legitimacy in the context of the EU.

title: The Law and Economics of Generative AI and Copyright A Primer to Core Challenges For Our Digital Future
affiliations: VU University Amsterdam - Faculty of Law, Tilburg Law and Economics Center (TILEC), University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne) and Technische Universität Berlin (TU Berlin), Weizenbaum Institute for the Networked Society

detail.title: The Law and Economics of Generative AI and Copyright A Primer to Core Challenges For Our Digital Future

publicationDetails.detailsText: forthcoming in Review of Network Economics

detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) systems raise fundamental challenges for copyright law at both the input and output stages. On the input side, legal uncertainty surrounds the large-scale scraping of copyrighted data for model training, with divergent rules across jurisdictions and limited transparency on how data is sourced. On the output side, courts struggle to determine when AI-assisted creations are sufficiently human to merit protection, leading to inconsistent or unclear legal outcomes. This paper outlines the "AI copyright conundrum" and examines its impact on the incentives to create, the accessibility of high-quality datasets, and the sustainability of cultural production. We discuss policy options and open questions for research.

title: Do Corrupt Practices Lead to Increased Cash Holdings in Firms? International Evidence
affiliations: University of South Australia - UniSA Business School, University of South Australia, University of South Australia and University of South Australia

detail.title: Do Corrupt Practices Lead to Increased Cash Holdings in Firms? International Evidence
detail.abstract: Using crosscountry firm-level data from 36 countries, we find that corrupt practices are associated with higher cash holdings. Further analysis suggests that corrupt firms are more constrained financially, motivating them to hold more cash. Our crosscountry results suggest that corrupt business practices are associated with higher cash holdings when institutional quality is better and is more market-oriented. Moreover, our evidence also suggests that corrupt behaviors and high cash holdings are more prominent among young firms and those with high capital expenditure and market to book ratio. Our results survive endogeneity tests and are robust to the use of alternate models and measures.

title: The Structure and Gender Differences in Overconfidence
affiliations: Lingnan College, Sun Yat-sen University, Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - Lingnan (University) College, Nanjing Audit University, Nanjing Audit University and Henan University of Economics and Law

detail.title: The Structure and Gender Differences in Overconfidence
detail.abstract: We study the sources of overconfidence and their gender differences across four dimensions: overoptimistic priors, overplacement, overprecision, and non-Bayesian updating. Overestimation of self-performance is widespread and stronger among men and low performers. Men also exhibit higher overplacement and overprecision. When receiving group performance feedback, men increase their overplacement, leading to even higher overestimation. Women, by contrast, ignore group feedback, showing little change in overestimation or overplacement. Therefore, men and women differ not only in the level of overconfidence but also in its sources and how they process information. When receiving personal feedback, both genders exhibit significant conservatism, underweighting feedback relative to Bayesian benchmarks. Moreover, conservatism increases as personal feedback becomes more informative. Thus, a sequence of less informative feedback may be more effective for debiasing than a single feedback with equivalent combined informativeness.
